title: Psalm 53:1–6
context: To the choirmaster: according to Mahalath. A Maskil of David. Near twin to Psalm 14: the fool denies God; all are corrupt; God looks for seekers and finds none who does good; oppressors devour the people; terror falls where none seemed due; Zion’s salvation is longed for.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Arminian and Reformed writers of the past on the fool’s denial, universal corruption, and salvation out of Zion, in their own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named. Calvin’s full exposition of this text is given with Psalm 14, to which Bible Hub’s Psalm 53 Calvin page points.

arminian.quote: Scattered—Hath not only broken their bones, their strength, and force, but also dispersed them hither and thither, so as there is no hope of a restoration. Thee—Against my people. Thou—Thou oh Jerusalem, which they besiege. The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. Corrupt are they, and have done abominable iniquity: there is none that doeth good.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Psalm 53)

reformed.quote: The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God: they have become corrupt, they have done abominable works: there is none that doeth good… David… teaches that the wickedness of men is so great, that they will never be brought to repentance, unless they are softened by the fear of God… When the Spirit of God inspires men with a desire to seek after God, it is then that they begin to understand… There did they tremble with fear… The prophet now encourages himself and all the faithful… that God will not forsake his people even to the end… when their affairs are in a state of the greatest tranquillity and prosperity, God will suddenly launch against them the bolts of his vengeance… Who shall give salvation to Israel out of Sion? … although God may leave us for a long time to languish, yet we ought not to weary… When the Lord shall have brought back the captivity of his people… God will not suffer the faithful to languish under continual sorrow.
reformed.source: Commentary on the Psalms (on Ps 14 / of Ps 53)

verses.text: The fool has said in his heart, “There is no God.” They are corrupt, and have done abominable iniquity. There is no one who does good.
verses.arminianNotes:
The fool has said in his heart, There is no God—corrupt, abominable iniquity—none who does good. Heart-atheism is practical: living as if God were absent. Corruption and abominable deeds follow the denial.

The fool’s verdict is chosen in the heart and issues in deeds. Grace confronts that denial; the hearer is summoned to seek God rather than settle into “no one who does good” as an excuse.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin (on this text via Ps 14): wickedness is so great men will not repent unless softened by the fear of God. “No one who does good” names the race apart from God’s people—corruption is native and universal, not a thin smear on otherwise sound seekers.

The fool’s heart-speech exposes depravity only grace can break. No God in the heart yields abominable life.
verses.keyContrast: Both confess heart-denial of God tied to corruption and “no one who does good.” Arminians underline the fool’s responsible heart-choice and the call still to seek God; Reformed Christians emphasize universal native corruption that only fear of God and regenerating grace interrupt.

verses.text: God looks down from heaven on the children of men, to see if there are any who understood, who seek after God.
verses.arminianNotes:
God looks down to see if any understood, who seek after God. Divine search for seekers—understanding shown in pursuit of God.

Seeking is the mark God looks for. The verse honors search; refusing to seek is the tragedy the next verse names.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: when the Spirit inspires desire to seek God, then understanding begins. God’s looking down exposes that apart from that work, the children of men do not seek.

Seeking is gift before it is achievement. God himself inspects whether anyone seeks.

verses.text: Every one of them has gone back. They have become filthy together. There is no one who does good, no, not one.
verses.arminianNotes:
All fallen away; together corrupt; none who does good, no, not one. Total in scope among those surveyed—no lone hero of goodness outside grace.

The indictment drives everyone to mercy. “Not one” removes boasting; it does not remove the duty to repent when grace calls.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin presses the universality: every one gone back, together filthy. Paul cites this line for the doctrine that all are under sin. Apart from the generation of the righteous, mankind is not partially sound.

Solidarity in corruption magnifies need of sovereign mercy. Not even one does good by nature.
verses.keyContrast: Both confess a sweeping “not one.” Arminians catch a leveling that drives all to resistible grace and repentance; Reformed Christians typically hear Pauline total inability apart from regenerating grace.

verses.text: Have the workers of iniquity no knowledge, who eat up my people as they eat bread, and don’t call on God?
verses.arminianNotes:
Workers of evil—no knowledge?—eat up my people as bread—do not call upon God. Oppression is casual as a meal; prayerlessness marks them.

Devouring the people and skipping prayer go together. Knowledge that should restrain is refused; call upon God instead of consuming the flock.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: God speaks in astonishment—those who ought to cherish his people fall on them like beasts. They have no more scruple than eating a morsel of bread. Sound understanding would restrain such cruelty; they do not call on the Lord.

Monstrous iniquity against the saints provokes heaven. Eating the people and prayerlessness are one disease.

verses.text: There they were in great fear, where no fear was, for God has scattered the bones of him who encamps against you. You have put them to shame, because God has rejected them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Great terror where no terror was; God scatters bones of the besieger; shame—God has rejected them. Wesley: Scattered—broken their strength and dispersed them with no hope of restoration. Thee—against my people. Thou—Jerusalem under siege.

God can overturn secure oppressors. Rejection is God’s verdict on those who encamped against his people.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: encourages the faithful—God will not forsake his people. Terror falls suddenly when the wicked think affairs most tranquil; God launches vengeance because he is with the generation of the righteous. Scattering bones of the besieger is deliverance as when a siege is broken.

Sudden judgment is providence for Zion’s defense. Both confess: shame follows God’s rejection of the encamped foe.

verses.text: Oh that the salvation of Israel would come out of Zion! When God brings back his people from captivity, then Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall be glad.
verses.arminianNotes:
Oh that Israel’s salvation would come from Zion! When God brings his people back, Jacob will rejoice and Israel will be glad. Longing prayer for national deliverance and joy.

Keep asking for Zion’s salvation. Restoration is God’s act; rejoicing is the people’s fitting response when fortunes turn.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: after consolation, return to prayer and groanings—do not weary though God leave us to languish. “Who shall give salvation?” is not despair of God’s hand. He will not suffer the faithful under continual sorrow; they that sow in tears shall reap in joy.

Delay does not void Zion’s promised gladness. Either reading: salvation out of Zion ends in Jacob’s joy.
verses.keyContrast: Both long for salvation out of Zion and joy at restored fortunes. Arminians emphasize persistent petition and glad response when God restores; Reformed commentators typically emphasize perseverance in prayer under delay, assured that God will not leave his captive people in endless sorrow.
